prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which opened the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: After reading the complete first-round exchange and the chair's questions, I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred configuration. The scientific core is a quantitative prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, flat bands at a magic angle, 2011) followed by an experimental discovery (correlated insulating and superconducting states, Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018) that the prediction alone did not guarantee. A single experimental knob, the twist angle, now tunes bandwidth and interaction strength, and independent groups have reproduced the phase diagram and carried it to other moire platforms. All eight round-1 files name B038 as a preferred configuration or alternative, and the six who prefer it agree on the same three names; I treat that as corroboration of the science, not as a substitute for it. My opening ranking placed circuit QED first and this configuration sixth. I moved because the arguments in round 1 about the 2025 overlap and the Girvin omission for B026 are ones I cannot answer from my own position, and because nobody disputes the central experimental observation. In answer to the chair's first question, my support does not depend on the pairing mechanism: the correlated insulators, the superconducting domes and their reproduction are the discovery, and a conventional mechanism would not remove them. I would accept the citation as drafted, anchored on the 2011 prediction and the 2018 observation, with no mechanism claimed.
statement.case_against: The microscopic origin of the superconductivity and parts of the correlated phase diagram remain unsettled, twist-angle disorder makes quantitative comparison between devices and laboratories weaker than for a measurement such as an optical clock, and the field is only about eight years old. Credit is also incomplete: Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and other moire groups cannot be represented within three names. Several of these priority statements, mine included, rest on recollection and have not been checked against sources in this exchange. Kroll and Lindroth make the best opposing case: B045 is mature, cleanly credited to two names and reproduced across national laboratories at the 1e-18 level, whereas B038 is younger and its attribution is more contested. If the committee concludes that the field needs several more years to separate robust physics from sample-specific behaviour, waiting would be defensible, and I record that as the argument I weigh most heavily against my own choice.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B045) have the cleanest two-name credit on the shortlist, are reproduced across national laboratories, and Kroll asks that a citation say what is specific to lattices as distinct from single-ion clocks and the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree the attribution and maturity of B045 are stronger than for B038, and I would support it if the committee wants a precision-measurement prize. My difficulty is the chair's question about new physics versus new accuracy. The case for lattice clocks as discovery rests on tests of relativity and constants and on many-body effects in clocks, but these are consequences that the clocks enable, not yet findings that changed how we understand a physical system, and ion clocks reach comparable uncertainty. The redefinition of the second has not happened and I would not count it as merit. I also take your point that the citation would have to state what a many-atom magic-wavelength lattice does that an ion does not. For those reasons B038 stays ahead for me, but B045 is my first alternative and the one I would vote for if B038 were judged premature.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is a new measurement regime with new physics in it, concedes the novelty and instrument-versus-discovery objections, and asks whether my low opening ranking of circuit QED reflected a view of its content or of the 2025 timing.
responses.response: A correction first: I ranked circuit QED first in my opening, not eighth, and B038 sixth, so my movement is toward B038. The reason for reducing B026 is partly timing, since the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits makes a close sequel hard to justify, and partly my own disclosure, because my work and my centre sit in this area. It is not a judgement against the physics of circuit QED. On your substantive argument, I accept that many-body effects in clocks and relativity tests at the 1e-18 level are real physics, and you make the discovery case for B045 better than the instrument label suggests. I still weigh it below a prediction-and-discovery sequence that opened a new area, but I regard that as a close judgement about weighting criteria, not a disagreement about the science, and I would not object to B045.

responses.point: Olsson takes the argument that B038 may be slightly early most seriously, citing sample-dependent claims, and asks what new physics as opposed to new accuracy the clocks have revealed.
responses.response: I share the concern about sample-specific claims, and it is why I would keep the citation to the platform, the flat-band prediction and the correlated and superconducting states, which are the parts reproduced by independent groups. I do not think this makes the discovery early: the phenomenology has been established in several laboratories and extended to other moire platforms, and the community learned to control disorder well enough for that. Where I think you are right is that we should not allow the citation to drift into claims about mechanism or about fractional states that are still being worked out. I also agree with your question to the clock supporters, and I have asked a version of it myself above. On the chair's question about a conventional pairing mechanism, I think the answer is that my support would not change, and I would like to hear whether yours would.

responses.point: Mehlig regards B038 as established by independent confirmation and extension to other moire platforms, and names B026 as the strongest fallback outside condensed matter if the committee wants distance from graphene.
responses.response: I agree that independent confirmation and the extension to other moire platforms are the right evidence for maturity, and they answer my own earlier hesitation. On your fallback, I would be cautious: you rank B026 fifth, and I am the member with the disclosed link to it, so I will not argue for it. If the committee needs a non-condensed-matter fallback, I would point to B045 first, because its credited set is clean and it has no overlap with the 2025 prize, while B026 carries both the overlap and the Girvin omission. I also note the competing packagings of topological insulators (B023 and B040) that you flag; I would not try to resolve them this year as long as B038 is available.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B038 on the breadth of support, records that the maturity concern would justify waiting, and would revisit B026 later.
responses.response: I appreciate that you separated the scientific argument from the vote count, which is how I think this should be done. I agree that the maturity of interpretation is the real reservation and not the reproducibility of the phenomenology. On B026, I would not ask the committee to revisit it soon; the 2025 overlap and the Girvin omission are fair obstacles, and my disclosure applies if it came to a ballot. Your own disclosure on B016 and the chair's question about recusals matter here: neither of us has a recorded link to B038 or B045, so our participation in a final choice between those two is not affected.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the roughly eight-year age of the field and the unresolved pairing mechanism as a reason to wait; I judge not, but it is a judgement about weighting.

Whether the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 experiments carry the decisive credit given Yuan Cao, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto; my account of the priority history is recalled and not checked against a source.
Whether lattice clocks have revealed new physics, as Kroll and Lindroth argue, or mainly new accuracy; if the committee decides they have, B045 would be an equally defensible choice.
Whether twist-angle disorder and sample-dependent behaviour will turn out to affect any of the robust claims on which the citation rests.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue on B026 (circuit QED) and, to a lesser degree, B007: I work in superconducting circuit and waveguide QED, direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology at Chalmers, have Chalmers colleagues (Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson) and frequent collaborators in this area, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I would recuse from a final decision on B026 if it came to a vote and would not argue for it. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B038 or B045, my preferred configuration and first alternative.
